passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?
passages.main_claim: Paying down high-interest credit card debt should be prioritized to save money in the long run.
passages.supporting_text: Most financial experts agree that the best practice is to pay down the balance on the highest interest card first, which may be able to save you more money in the long run. The faster you can tackle your highest interest card, the less interest and fees you accrue.
conditions: You have high-interest credit card debt.
You can make larger payments towards your debt.
caveats: Focusing solely on debt repayment may deplete your savings.
It may be easier to pay off lower balance cards for psychological benefits.

passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?
passages.main_claim: Paying off debt first may be beneficial when you carry high-interest credit card debt.
passages.supporting_text: High-interest debt costs you more than most savings accounts will earn. When you knock out those balances, you gain room in your budget and can allocate that money towards other debt or save for a goal.
conditions: Your debts keep you from meeting basic needs.
You already have a small emergency fund set aside.
caveats: Be sure to keep paying all minimums on time.
You may want to consider putting your extra money toward the highest-interest or highest balance account first.

passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?
passages.main_claim: Paying down high-interest debt is crucial for improving financial health.
passages.supporting_text: Even if you're keeping up with monthly payments, chipping away at higher-interest debt can go a long way toward improving your financial health. Having manageable debt lets you focus on a long-term savings plan.
conditions: You have high-interest debt.
You can prioritize debt repayment in your budget.
caveats: The best method for paying off debt depends on your personal situation.
Paying debt over a longer period may result in more interest paid.

passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?

passages.supporting_text: Credit cards and some personal loans can carry double-digit interest rates that make it easy for your debt to build up. The Fed has also begun raising interest rates, which will impact the cost of borrowing.

passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?
passages.main_claim: It is important to build an emergency fund to ensure financial stability and avoid using credit for unexpected expenses.
passages.supporting_text: Emergency funds have several benefits - most notably the financial stability they provide. If you have enough saved in your emergency fund, you will have more confidence when you encounter surprise expenses. Additionally, emergency funds will help you avoid using credit or loans to cover costs and can give you more flexibility in how and when you make payments.
conditions: You have enough savings to cover necessary expenses.
You can consistently set aside money each month.
caveats: Unexpected expenses can still arise, requiring careful planning.

passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?
passages.main_claim: It may make sense to prioritize building an emergency fund before aggressively paying down debt.
passages.supporting_text: Without savings, you're vulnerable to any financial disruption, which could force you into more debt. Establishing a modest emergency fund - say $500 to $1,000 to start - can prevent future financial setbacks and give you some breathing room.
conditions: If you don't have an emergency fund
If your debt isn't urgent or costly
caveats: Using savings to pay off debt can leave you without a financial cushion for emergencies.

passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?
passages.main_claim: An emergency fund should be established before aggressively paying off debt to protect against unexpected expenses.
passages.supporting_text: Having an emergency fund is critical in the event you get hit with unexpected expenses - for example, you suddenly need to replace your computer, have your car repaired, or pay for emergency medical care. Having cash on hand for unexpected circumstances can help you avoid borrowing money and incurring potentially costly debt.

passages.query: Should I build an emergency fund or pay down credit card debt first?
passages.main_claim: Building an emergency fund is important even if you have debt to pay down.
passages.supporting_text: An emergency fund could help you overcome sudden financial challenges. Whether budget pressures stem from higher costs, a job loss, or an unexpected expense, they can appear without warning. Saving in advance of such events is critical, even as you pay down debt.
conditions: You may have manageable debt.

caveats: Fewer than half of Americans have enough savings to cover three months of expenses.

passages.main_claim: Building an emergency fund is essential to protect yourself from unexpected financial emergencies.
passages.supporting_text: Setting up a dedicated savings or emergency fund is one essential way to protect yourself, and it's one of the first steps you can take to start saving. passages.main_claim: You should prioritize building an emergency fund before aggressively paying down debt.
passages.supporting_text: If you need to build your emergency fund from scratch, then your first goal should be to save one month's worth of living expenses. This amount should give you some breathing room and allow you to cover a minor emergency. Imagine if you begin aggressively paying down your debt, but you have nothing set aside for emergencies. passages.supporting_text: The choice of debt repayment or savings is not an either-or proposition. Automate savings right off the top through payroll deduction and direct deposit, then use take-home pay to maximize the debt repayment effort.
